content: Surgical site infections (SSIs) are more common in liver transplantation compared to other types of solid organ transplantation. Studies have reported that the incidence of SSIs after liver transplantation ranges from 8.8% to 37.5%. This highlights the importance of antimicrobial prophylaxis as a potential strategy to reduce these infections. However, there is currently insufficient evidence in the medical literature to identify the most effective prophylactic antibiotic regimen for liver transplantation. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and potential harms of different antibiotic prophylactic regimens in preventing SSIs in patients undergoing liver transplantation. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Science Citation Index Expanded, and LILACS. The most recent search was completed on September 11, 2015. The inclusion criteria for this review encompassed all randomized clinical trials comparing any antibiotic regimen to placebo, no intervention, or another antibiotic regimen in liver transplant recipients, regardless of age, sex, or the underlying reason for transplantation. Quasi-randomized studies and observational studies were also considered for data on potential harms if they were identified during the search for randomized trials. Two authors independently selected relevant studies, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. The search yielded 786 publications after duplicates were removed. However, only one study, which was published in abstract form, met the inclusion criteria. This trial was conducted at the Shiraz Transplant Centre in Shiraz, Iran, and involved 180 consecutive liver transplant recipients who were randomly assigned to one of two antibiotic regimens. The trial was judged to have a high risk of bias. The study authors reported that 163 participants were included in the final analysis after randomization, suggesting that 17 high-risk liver transplant recipients were excluded. The trial compared two antibiotic regimens: ceftriaxone plus metronidazole versus ampicillin-sulbactam plus ceftizoxime. The authors of the trial concluded that there were no significant differences between the two regimens in terms of their effectiveness. However, no numerical data were provided, and the review authors were unable to independently verify the findings due to the lack of trial data. In conclusion, the benefits and harms of antibiotic prophylactic regimens for preventing SSIs in liver transplantation remain uncertain. There is a need for additional well-designed randomized clinical trials that adhere to established guidelines, such as SPIRIT and CONSORT, to clarify the role of antibiotic prophylaxis in this patient population.
